The laboratory should have the following equipment and consumables: autoclave, water purification system, clinical centrifuge (3000 rpm), incubator, freezer (-70°C, optional), freezer (-20°C), refrigerator (4–8°C), disposable gloves, disposable lab coats, disposable pipette tips, disposable serological pipettes, computer with printer, internet connection (1-year subscription), ELISA plate washer, ELISA plate incubator (37°C), ELISA plate reader (capable of reading at 405 nm, 450 nm, 490 nm, and reference at 630 nm), automatic pipetters (P10, P100, P1000), multichannel automatic pipetters (P10, P100, P1000), pipette aid for serological pipettes, and a timer. 2. The laboratory must have standard operating procedures (SOPs) for a quality management system, approved by the laboratory director and quality manager. These SOPs should cover the pre-analytical, analytical, and post-analytical phases, including test requests, test selection, personnel training, patient preparation, specimen collection, labeling, transport, processing, storage, reagent preparation, equipment maintenance, quality control, test performance, proficiency testing, external quality assessment, result transcription, reporting, record maintenance, and laboratory accreditation. 3. The laboratory should specify the types of specimens, screening tests, and confirmatory tests used, along with their performance characteristics, including sensitivity, specificity, cost per test, and field use. Information should be based on laboratory records, package inserts, inventory, and material safety data sheets. 4. Biomarker surveys are the reference method to estimate the prevalence of infections with hepatitis viruses. These surveys are critical for monitoring and evaluating hepatitis elimination efforts, assessing the impact of universal HBV immunization, and guiding public health interventions. 5. For hepatitis D virus (HDV), testing for HDV biomarkers should be considered if HDV co-infection is of public health importance among HBV-infected patients. For hepatitis A virus (HAV), seroprevalence surveys by age group can guide decisions on including HAV vaccines in routine immunization schedules. For hepatitis E virus (HEV), antibody prevalence by age group can help interpret acute hepatitis E rates and guide prevention and control measures. 6. The user guide for the template protocol aims to assist survey implementers in adapting the protocol to their local settings. The target audience includes viral hepatitis program managers, immunization program managers, primary investigators of biomarker surveys, and public health officials providing technical assistance. 7. The protocol template provides guidance for developing a survey protocol, including reviewing local epidemiology, WHO guidance documents, and previous surveys; organizing stakeholder meetings; adapting the protocol to local needs; seeking peer review; obtaining ethics clearance; and providing feedback to WHO. 8. The protocol should include a clear title specifying the biomarkers tested, population, timing, and geographical area. Investigators and their roles, funding sources, and permissions from national data protection agencies should also be included. 9. The background section should provide information on viral hepatitis, local epidemiology, vaccination schedules, testing strategies, and policies guided by the study results. Study objectives should address public health policies and align with international reporting standards. 10. The survey design should be cross-sectional, with defined populations and exclusion criteria. Sampling procedures should prioritize random sampling or cluster surveys to optimize resources and minimize bias. Convenience sampling is unacceptable for verifying regional hepatitis B control goals. 11. Data collection should involve trained teams, logistics for specimen storage and transport, and appropriate data collection tools. Blood specimens should be stored and transported separately from vaccines or medicines. Testing strategies must follow WHO guidelines. 12. Analysis plans should include double data entry to minimize errors, descriptive analysis to clean datasets, and consideration of sampling design and weights. Quality assurance measures should be described to ensure data reliability and validity.
